extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and scholars of literary theory, semiotics, and creative writing
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and apply Roland Barthes's concepts and methods for analyzing texts, images, and cultural phenomena; useful for critics, theorists, and writers seeking Barthesian criteria for interpretation and composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readerly vs Writerly text
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between texts that make no requirement of the reader (readerly) and texts that make the reader an active producer of meaning (writerly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readerly texts present 'ready-made' meanings and uphold common sense/Doxa; writerly texts 'make the reader no longer a consumer but a producer of the text' and open plurality of entrances, networks, and languages. Aim for texts that require active interpretation rather than passive consumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Death of the Author
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejects the notion of authorial intention as the ultimate source of meaning; the author's biography/intentions are not the anchor for interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive horizons should be opened: meaning is proliferated in language and created by readers. Avoid grounding critical judgments solely in presumed authorial intent; prioritize textual and readerly production of meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five codes (S/Z) / use of lexia
rubrics_metrics.description: Barthes's S/Z method establishes five major codes for determining various kinds of significance and uses 'lexia' (arbitrarily chosen text units) for analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break the text into lexias to remain methodologically unbiased; apply the five codes to reveal plurality of meaning. Use this coding method to show how different signifying systems operate within the narrative and to map openings for multiple readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal text: reversibility and openness
rubrics_metrics.description: An ideal (writerly) text is reversible or open to the greatest variety of independent interpretations rather than restrictive in meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid restrictive devices (e.g., strict timelines, exact definitions of events) that limit interpretive freedom. Compose texts that permit multiple, independent readings and resist closure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural analysis: functions, actions, narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative can be analysed hierarchically into 'functions' (elementary pieces, e.g., descriptive words), 'actions' (characters/events formed from functions), and the larger 'narrative'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this breakdown to evaluate how functions combine to create actions and gauge the realism or authenticity of a narrative. Assess whether key functions suitably generate believable actions and whether the narrative's structure supports its claims about reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myth as two levels of signification
rubrics_metrics.description: Myth results from two levels of signification: the first-order 'language-object' (literal meaning) and the second-order 'metalanguage' (the myth or connotation imposed on the first-order sign).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In cultural criticism, identify the signifier/signified pair on the first level and then uncover the second-order connotation that naturalizes ideology. Example: a bottle (signifier) denotes wine (signified) but connotes healthy, robust national identity in bourgeois myth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semiotic methods (commutation, paradigmatic and syntagmatic analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use semiotic tools—commutation tests, paradigmatic and syntagmatic analysis—to dissect sign systems and reveal how meanings are constructed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply commutation tests (swap elements to see meaning change) and examine paradigmatic choices and syntagmatic relations to expose ideological operations and the mechanism of signification in texts, images, and cultural objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutral writing and The Pleasure of the Text (jouissance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Barthes's aim for neutral writing: language that is open, noncommittal, and avoids loaded labels; reading that leads to 'jouissance'—a blissful, immersive loss of self within the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for prose that resists asserting fixed identities or ideological labels; cultivate a mode of writing/reading that produces aesthetic immersion rather than didactic assertions. Be aware that even 'neutral' words can be taken assertively by context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doxa vs Para-doxa
rubrics_metrics.description: Doxa: the unacknowledged systems of meaning through which culture is absorbed (official, limiting language). Para-doxa: the opposing or marginal mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique and avoid Doxa's limiting, naturalizing language in both analysis and composition; seek para-doxic approaches that resist cultural assimilation and challenge conventional meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author vs Scriptor (intertextuality emphasis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace the traditional 'author' figure with the 'scriptor'—a writer whose role is to recombine pre-existing texts and conventions rather than originate meaning ex nihilo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus analysis and creative practice on intertextual relations, conventions, and prior texts that inform a work. De-emphasize biographical or intentionalist explanations in favour of textual and cultural linkages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographic meaning: studium and punctum
rubrics_metrics.description: In photography, studium refers to the general, cultural, symbolic interest of an image; punctum is the personally piercing detail that wounds or pricks the viewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating photographs, identify both the studium (shared cultural readings) and the punctum (subjective, affective detail). Recognize that punctum is personal and can resist translation into a fully social or symbolic logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cultural criticism to reveal ideology (demystification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Barthes's method in Mythologies: interrogate everyday cultural materials to expose how bourgeois society asserts values through them; cultural signs are never neutral but embedded in ideological structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze commonplace objects, adverts, media, and practices to decode how narratives and signs function as tools of ideological reproduction. Use examples (cars, advertisements, magazine covers, toys) to show how meanings naturalize social values.
